title: Checkpoint: Early Music
objective: After this level you can trace music from bone flutes to Renaissance polyphony.
summary: The Seikilos epitaph, carved with its melody on a tombstone, is the oldest complete song. The chapter runs from bone flutes through chant, notation and polyphony to print.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: the oldest complete song you can still sing.
cards.body: It's carved on a marble tombstone from ancient Tralles, near Aydın in Turkey, and its tune survives because someone wrote the notes above the words. That idea, getting music out of memory and onto something lasting, runs through this whole chapter.

cards.headline: A song on a tombstone
cards.body: The Seikilos epitaph, dated to the 1st or 2nd century CE, is widely considered the oldest complete musical composition; older notated pieces survive only in fragments. Greek letters and signs above its words give the melody. The words say: while you live, shine; have no grief at all; life is short. Found in 1883, it's now in the National Museum of Denmark.

mascot.line: Shine while you live. Not bad advice, from a tombstone.

cards.headline: The chapter in one breath
cards.body: Music began in memory: bone flutes, sung verses, chant learned by ear. Writing it down let melodies outlast their singers, and Guido's staff let people read tunes they'd never heard. Troubadours show the cost of not writing: most of their melodies are gone. Then voices multiplied, from one line of chant to Pérotin's four, and printing, from Venice in 1501, took polyphony off the scribe's desk.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How writing music down moved it from memory to the page, and why most troubadour tunes were lost.
What bone flutes, Greek string ratios and Chinese bronze bells reveal about music's deep past.
How singing grew from chant's single line into several independent voices at once.
Why printing music from movable type spread songs to singers across Europe.

questions.prompt: The Seikilos epitaph, the oldest complete composition, survives carved on what?

options.label: A bone flute
options.rationale: Flutes are instruments; the Seikilos song is words and melody.

options.label: A papyrus scrap
options.rationale: That's how a few lines of Euripides' Orestes survive.

options.label: A bronze bell
options.rationale: The Zeng bells carry music theory, not this song.

questions.explanation: The Seikilos song is carved, with its melody, on a marble tombstone from ancient Tralles.

questions.prompt: Why can the Seikilos song still be sung, when most troubadour songs can't?

options.label: Its words were in Greek
options.rationale: Language isn't the issue; the tune is.

options.label: Its melody was written above its words
It was taught in every Greek theater
options.rationale: Nothing says it was performed there.

questions.explanation: Notation carved above the words preserves its melody; most troubadour poems were copied without their tunes.

questions.prompt: From Level 21: what are the oldest widely accepted musical instruments?

options.label: Bone and ivory flutes from German caves
The Divje Babe bone from Slovenia
options.rationale: Its holes may be hyena bites, so it's disputed.

options.label: The Zeng bronze bells
options.rationale: They're about 2,400 years old: ancient, but far younger.

options.label: The Greek aulos
options.rationale: The flutes are tens of thousands of years older.

questions.explanation: Flutes from Geissenklösterle (42,000 to 43,000 years) and Hohle Fels (over 35,000) are the oldest accepted instruments.

questions.prompt: From Level 27's Notre-Dame story: what did Pérotin add to organum?

options.label: A second voice, for the first time
options.rationale: Organum had two voices long before Pérotin.

options.label: Parts for three and four voices

questions.explanation: When church music was almost all two-part, Pérotin wrote organa for three and four voices.
